On an autumn morning, Mina and her grandfather Tomas begin a year of walking through the forest.
The oak lets its acorns fall, and Tomas explains that each acorn is a seed.
A jay buries acorns, and the ones it forgets may grow into new oaks.
Mina finds one acorn in the soil and marks the spot to watch it through the year.
Leaves change colour in autumn as the green chlorophyll breaks down.
A tree seals the base of each leaf and lets it fall to survive the winter.
Worms, beetles and fungi break down fallen leaves and turn them into soil.
Tomas describes the layers of a forest: canopy, understorey and floor.
Bark works like skin, protecting the living wood from cold, insects and sometimes fire.
A tree adds one ring of wood each year, so the rings tell its age.
Wide rings usually mean good years and narrow rings hard years, so rings record the weather.
Snow falls, and the forest rests through winter.
Evergreens keep narrow, waxy needles through winter.
Many seeds need a spell of cold before they sprout, so the acorn waits.
Animals live through winter, and squirrels forget nuts that may sprout.
Buds already hold the folded leaves of next spring.
A standing dead tree gives homes and food to many creatures.
Tomas shows Mina the fungal threads around roots, called mycorrhizal.
Trees and fungi trade sugar for water and minerals.
Fungal threads can join trees, and scientists have measured substances moving between them.
Suzanne Simard and others studied old hub trees, and some scientists think these may help seedlings.
Scientists still disagree about how much the networks matter in a whole forest.
Spring arrives, sap rises and the buds swell.
Mina's acorn splits open and a root pushes out first.
Root hairs take in water and minerals.
Roots sense wetter soil and spread wide and shallow.
A shoot rises into the deep shade, and seedlings may wait there for light.
The big oak opens its new leaves.
Photosynthesis turns light, water and carbon dioxide into sugar and releases oxygen.
Tiny pores called stomata let gases in and out and let water vapour escape.
Water climbs through the xylem, pulled by evaporation from the leaves.
Sugar travels down through the phloem, just under the bark.
Spring fills the branches with nesting birds, bees and wind-blown oak pollen.
Caterpillars eat young leaves, and trees defend themselves with chemicals.
Some trees release chemicals when chewed, and neighbours may respond, though scientists debate what it means.
The same chemicals may attract wasps and birds that attack the caterpillars.
In midsummer, the forest is cooler than the fields outside.
A summer storm shows that wind makes trees thicker and stronger.
An old fire scar shows how some trees and plants survive and recover.
The storm has felled a giant beech and opened a gap of light.
The fallen tree decays slowly and feeds new life.
Tomas tells Mina about the bristlecone pines, the oldest known trees.
Tomas tells Mina about the coast redwoods, the tallest trees.
Autumn returns, and Mina sees the forest as a connected community.
Mina's seedling has survived the year but is still very small.
Trees store carbon, and forests matter for the climate.
Forests also shelter animals, hold soil and keep water clean.
People can plant the right trees in the right places and protect old forests.
Tomas gives two rules: leave deadwood, and walk lightly.
Mina plants her own acorn, joining the long work of the forest.
